entry.title: Make It So: Election Night Was the Easy Part
entry.summary: Patrick Stewart is gone, and a wave of first-time leaders just got elected. Waves don't fail at the ballot box — they fail in the months after. Here's the arithmetic of the next election nobody is talking about, and a small Python tool for the work that comes after.
entry.content:
The first leader I ever wanted to be was bald, British and fictional.

Jean-Luc Picard.

I was a kid on a carpet in Illinois, blanket in my fists, and he made me believe I could lead something someday.

Five days before election night, Patrick Stewart died at 86. He was my Captain.

Picard's gift wasn't being in charge. It was getting everyone on his bridge ready to be. He listened. He asked his officers what they thought, and he meant it. He trusted the people others overlooked. And when the talking was done, he made a decision and owned it.

Make it so.

Stewart didn't only play that. As a boy he watched his father abuse his mother, and he spent the rest of his life working against it: as a patron of Refuge, the domestic violence charity, since 2007, for his mother, and with Combat Stress, the veterans' mental health charity, for his father, who came home from the war with shell shock, what we would now call PTSD. About his mother, he said:

I couldn't help her then. Now I can.

Not in a year when it trended. Not for a news cycle. For nearly twenty years.

That is the whole lesson, and it is the only one this post has.

I've been thinking about it this week, because on Tuesday a lot of new people were handed the conn.

A wave of firsts

The 2026 midterms put people into high office who had, until now, mostly been kept at the edges. Across both parties, voters elected:

  • Deb Haaland in New Mexico, the first Native American woman elected governor of any U.S. state.
  • Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, the first Black woman elected governor of any state.
  • Chris Pappas of New Hampshire, the first out gay man elected to the U.S. Senate.
  • Julia Letlow of Louisiana, the state's first Republican woman elected to the Senate.
  • Gina Hinojosa, Texas's first Latina governor.
  • Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, the first Native American woman elected to the U.S. Senate.
  • Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate.
  • Melat Kiros of Colorado, the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress, at 29.

The records are not only about who ran. At least 159 women will serve in the 120th Congress, a new high, past the record of 152 set in 2024, and at least 136 in the House, 31.3% of it. Black women and Latinas both set new records for congressional representation. At least 17 women will be governors, 34% of the country's governorships, past the old record of 14. Georgia, Minnesota, Ohio and Tennessee elected a woman governor for the first time. (A few races were still too close to call when I wrote this, so some of those counts may still move.)

Young people turned out too. CIRCLE at Tufts estimates 27% of young people voted, the second-highest midterm youth turnout in thirty years, and about 30% in battleground states. It's an early estimate; CIRCLE will update it in spring 2027 once voter files are in.

That said, the trends do not all run one way. Women's representation in the Senate goes down next year, from 27 to at least 23. And fourteen states have still never had a woman governor at all.

While those are the numbers, what it felt like to me was a song.

I grew up dancing to "Bidi Bidi Bom Bom" after watching the Selena movie with my cousin Amy and my sister Erin, who — I will die on this hill — reminds me of and is my Selena. We watched it for the first time at my abuela's house.

On Tuesday night, they played "Como la Flor" at Gina Hinojosa's victory party.

I saw three people at once. The kid on the carpet. Me now. And whoever is small right now and is going to grow up with a Latina governor of Texas as the ordinary picture of what a governor looks like.

This post isn't about who won. It's about what comes next, and about who is walking into rooms they — or the people they represent — may never have been in before.

Go ahead and dance. I did. The firsts are real, they took decades, and anyone who tells you not to celebrate them has never waited for one.

And one of them is my aunt

Mary Mesa was elected to the Lake County Board in District 17, by about five points. She is one of the most inspiring leaders I know, and she just won a seat most people in her area probably couldn't name.

Nineteen people sit on that board. They approve the county budget and every financial matter that reaches county government, in a county that contains 219 separate taxing bodies — municipalities, townships, school districts, park districts, libraries, fire districts. Courts and public safety run on what those nineteen vote for.

I can't name all of my own local representatives. But I can tell you who makes me want to be more involved. My Aunt Mary saw something and decided to do something about it.

That is the room this whole post is about.

The question history will actually ask

Here's the part nobody puts on a victory banner: election day is one day. Representation is every day after it.

Someday someone will write the history of the 2026 midterms. The only open question is whether the last chapter is about the people who got elected — or the people who kept showing up.

Because waves don't fail at the ballot box. They fail in the months after, when everyone who turned out once decides the work is done.

I learned that the slow way, in open source. I ran for the Python Software Foundation's Board of Directors and got a seat right away, which was luck. The part that wasn't luck took years: reading bylaws, reviewing grants, hunting for funding, sending email across every time zone to volunteers who were all doing it after their day jobs, and thanking the community for feedback I did not always enjoy hearing — then trying to be better. Then rotating out so someone new could rotate in. Getting elected was the easy part.

PyLadies Chicago taught me the same lesson on a smaller scale. Saying "welcome" never kept a new organizer. What kept them was the rest of us showing up, month after month, until the room felt like theirs.

Scale that up and the clock only gets longer. In 2008, after she lost the nomination, Hillary Clinton said the highest, hardest glass ceiling had about 18 million cracks in it. It took eighteen more years for a Black woman to be elected governor of any state.

A first is not a finish. People hold a seat because the people who put them there stay in the room.

Closer to home: 108 days

Chicago's next municipal election is February 23, 2027. As I write this, on November 7, that is 108 days away.

On that ballot: mayor, city clerk, city treasurer, all fifty alderpersons, and the Police District Councils in each of the city's 22 police districts. If nobody clears a majority, a runoff follows on April 6.

Now the arithmetic. In November 2024, Chicago turnout was 67.94%. In the February 2023 municipal election — the one that picked every alderperson in the city — it was 35.85%.

The people who decide whether your street gets plowed, where a zoning variance lands, and what your ward does with its menu money are chosen by barely half the crowd that shows up to pick a president.

The same numbers as a table
YearPresidential generalYearChicago municipal
198478.23%198382.07%
198871.58%198774.08%
199274.57%199145.06%
199663.17%199542.25%
200070.22%199941.92%
200475.13%200333.71%
200873.87%200733.08%
201275.41%201142.30%
201671.04%201534.03%
202073.28%201935.45%
202467.94%202335.85%

Chicago is not a city that cannot be bothered. In April 1983 a municipal election here drew 82.07% — higher than any presidential general in this chart. The ceiling is not the problem. The habit is.

This is not a Chicago quirk. It's the design. Sarah Anzia's Timing and Turnout (University of Chicago Press, 2014) found that off-cycle elections don't lower everyone's turnout equally — they lower it among people with no particular stake, while organized groups keep voting. The smaller the electorate, the larger the share those groups represent. The Public Policy Institute of California puts the gap at roughly 36 percentage points between off-cycle city elections and those held alongside a presidential race.

Low turnout isn't apathy. It's a room with the lights dimmed, and somebody already sitting in it.

Tuesday proved it cuts both ways

Here's the hopeful part, and it happened on the same ballot as the firsts.

Keisha Lance Bottoms said it on election night, after an opponent who had spent nearly $200 million of his own money trying to beat her. In her words:

You've shown that no amount of money will ever never ever ever overcome the power of the people.

She was talking about her own campaign. It was true somewhere much smaller on the same night.

Ballotpedia counted 41 local data center measures on the November 3 ballot across ten states. Ohio alone had 21, across 18 jurisdictions. In Sunbury, residents passed a charter amendment restricting data centers drawing 25 megawatts or more. In Wilmington, about 80% of voters rejected all four rezoning referendums that would have rezoned rural residential land for industrial use.

These were township zoning questions and charter amendments — the least-covered rooms in American government. And they just became the place where the largest infrastructure buildout of our lifetime gets decided.

I want to be careful here, because I write about AI and I build with it. This isn't a story about technology losing. It's a story about who gets a vote on where it goes, and what it costs them. Those are the rooms where that gets settled, and for one Tuesday, people filled them.

(These counts were unofficial at the time of writing; I'll update them once they're certified.)

The Duty Roster

So I built the smallest possible thing that helps.

It's a roster: every election between now and 2028, plus the rooms that meet without a ballot — Police District Council meetings, Local School Council meetings, your ward office, Chi Hack Night. Each row lists when it happens, what it governs, the turnout the last comparable election drew, and where every one of those facts came from.

Each row has a button that says Make it so. It downloads a calendar file. Where a schedule belongs to your district, school or ward, the button says Find yours and goes to the official page instead.

That's the whole product. No account, no server, no API key. A pledge decays; a calendar entry goes off on February 23 whether or not you still feel like it.

I didn't copy the election dates from anywhere. The Illinois Election Code sets them by rule, so the code computes them from the law and checks them against the State Board of Elections' published calendar:

import calendar
from datetime import date, timedelta

TUESDAY = calendar.TUESDAY


def last_weekday(year: int, month: int, weekday: int) -> date:
    last = date(year, month, calendar.monthrange(year, month)[1])
    return last - timedelta(days=(last.weekday() - weekday) % 7)


def consolidated_primary(year: int) -> date:
    """10 ILCS 5/2A-1.1: odd years, the last Tuesday in February.
    Chicago's mayor, clerk, treasurer and all 50 alderpersons are elected that day."""
    return last_weekday(year, 2, TUESDAY)


assert consolidated_primary(2023) == date(2023, 2, 28)  # the last one, per the election board
assert consolidated_primary(2027) == date(2027, 2, 23)  # the next one, per the State Board
# full implementation, with tests and every source: github.com/lorenanicole/blog-code/tree/main/make-it-so-show-up-build-tools

The calendar files follow the iCalendar standard (RFC 5545) to the letter, commas escaped and all, so any standards-following calendar app can open them. Each one is about a dozen lines of plain text. A dozen lines is the difference between remembering and forgetting.

Every number on the roster carries its source: turnout from the Chicago Board of Election Commissioners' official proclamations, meeting schedules from the City, CPS and the organizers themselves. A small script re-reads those pages to make sure the facts still hold. It asks each site's robots.txt for permission first, identifies itself, waits between requests, and touches nothing but public pages. No personal data goes in or comes out.

Meanwhile, YouTube keeps serving me ads for dollar stores, Starlink and how to ride the CTA. The unsettling part is that it's mostly right. I do shop the dollar store, and I always need help with the CTA. It knows because it watches. The roster doesn't, and won't.

Open the Duty Roster: five ballots and four rooms, each one sourced.

Not a code person? Download the roster as a PDF to print, stick on the fridge, or forward to your group chat. Every link and date is in it.

Engage

Picard didn't end a briefing with a speech. He ended it with one word.

Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed ended his victory speech Tuesday night with six: "So Michigan, let's go build it."

Same beat. The talking is done, and the work starts now.

So here's my ask. Pick your post:

  • Gold, operations. One project. Chi Hack Night has been building civic tech in Chicago for years. Bring a laptop.
  • Blue, sciences. One person. Mentor someone new, especially someone who's the first in their family, their team or their office to do the thing.
  • Red, command. One meeting. A ward night, a school council, a police district council. Show up when there's no ballot on the table.

Then put the next one on your calendar before you close this tab. That's the only part that compounds.

The firsts got elected. Whether they get to govern is a question about day 108, and the runoff in April, and every quiet meeting in between.

Until next time: live long, Python & prosper. 🖖

entry.title: Grace Hopper Didn't Wait for Permission. Neither Should We.
entry.summary: GHC is canceled. The way we work, hire and learn in tech has changed, and how we invest in community is changing with it. Here's where the energy goes next, starting with PyLadiesCon on December 5–7.
entry.content:
Two weeks. That's how much notice the community got.

The Grace Hopper Celebration, slated for October 27–30 in Anaheim, is canceled. AnitaB.org's notice is candid about why: individual registrations and sponsorship commitments both came in well under expectations, and under what it takes to keep the lights on. Flights are booked. Talks are written. Hotel deposits are sitting on credit cards. And thousands of women, many of them students who were counting on GHC for their first real shot at a recruiter's attention, just lost one of the biggest rooms they had.

AnitaB.org's own notice names what's at stake: travel booked, hotels reserved, visas granted, time off approved, teams organized. (If that's you: the notice asks you to cancel flights and hotels directly with your providers, says registrants will hear about registration fees by October 26, and routes questions to GHC@AnitaB.org.)

For a lot of women in this career, "Grace Hopper" was more than a conference. It was a destination. You heard about it from a professor, a manager, the senior engineer who'd been. Getting there was a milestone. Over the years, my own connection to AnitaB.org ran through its local chapters, the smaller rooms where a few dozen women in tech actually got to know each other. When I was just starting out in tech, I taught workshops there on object-oriented programming in Ruby and Python.

That's the duality worth naming. GHC was the name brand, the place everyone knew. But belonging was built year-round in chapters, meetups, Slacks and DMs from mentors. Losing the destination hurts. Whether we keep investing in everything around it is what decides what happens next.

I want to be clear about one thing before going further: this isn't a pile-on. Running a conference at GHC's scale is brutal, and the people who built it gave a generation of women in computing a place to belong. But I've spent a decade building distributed systems and a decade building community, and from both seats I see the same pattern: when the work changes, the architecture evolves.

From monolith to network

GHC has - arguably - been the biggest room for women-in-tech, but it was never the only one. More than 700 companies participate each year, per Forbes. For a lot of companies, "supporting women in tech" quietly collapsed into one line item: sponsor GHC, send recruiters, post the booth photo.

How big is big? AnitaB.org says GHC grew from 630 attendees in 2002 to more than 22,000 in 2018, and last year's Chicago edition drew over 20,000 participants (AnitaB.org marketed it as 30,000+). That's enormous. But it isn't alone at the top. The Society of Women Engineers' WE24, also in Chicago, drew 19,114 people, and SWE bills its own conference as the world's largest for women and allies in engineering and technology. "Largest" depends on who's counting and which lane you're in.

Any engineer knows this pattern. Plenty of great systems start as a monolith, and that's not a mistake: it's how you get something big off the ground. But as the work grows and changes, you break it into services that can scale, evolve and run on their own. That's not a teardown. It's a refactor.

And the change reaches beyond one event. In the full notice, CEO Brenda Darden Wilkerson writes that GHC has been central to AnitaB.org's mission and that the circumstances behind the cancellation have hurt the organization's finances. AnitaB.org is now weighing strategic alternatives and what programming it can offer going forward, with more announcements expected in the coming weeks. When one big event is also the funding model, a shift in that event reshapes the whole organization.

And the timing matters. Women held about 27.5% of U.S. computer and mathematical jobs last year, per Forbes' read of BLS data, and the gap is widest exactly where the industry is heading next.

When budgets tighten, diversity spend treated as marketing is the first thing cut. That's not a GHC problem. That's an us problem.

The AI double bind

Here's why this lands differently in 2026 than it would have in 2016. AI is where the jobs, the money and the leverage are going, and women are getting squeezed from three sides at once.

  • Building it. Women made up just 26% of U.S. AI hires in 2025, versus 50% of hires into non-AI roles, per LinkedIn. Across 27 countries, they hold only 13% of C-suite AI leadership roles at AI companies. Stanford's 2026 AI Index, as summarized by Forbes, found no country at gender parity among AI researchers and developers, and no meaningful progress since 2010.
  • Being displaced by it. In high-income countries, jobs at the highest risk of generative-AI automation make up 9.6% of women's employment, versus 3.5% of men's, according to the ILO. The study's lead author told World Politics Review that if those jobs vanished, two women would be displaced for every man.
  • Using it. A meta-analysis of 18 studies covering more than 140,000 people found women roughly 20% less likely than men to use generative AI, and the gap held even when access was equalized.

Meanwhile, U.S. AI job postings have roughly doubled since 2023, per the same LinkedIn research. The opportunity is growing. Women's share of it doesn't have to stay where it is.

And look at what the research says drives the usage gap: familiarity, confidence, training. Someone to learn alongside. That isn't a recruiting booth. That's a workshop, a sprint, a mentor, a chapter meetup on a Tuesday night. It's exactly what community spaces like PyLadies do, and exactly what disappears when we treat them as optional.

The comments section already knows

Want the ground-level view? Read the r/csMajors thread. The top comment asks whether employers simply aren't hiring, so they aren't paying for booths. The original poster guesses sponsors saw weak ROI as attendance dropped. Others point out it's expensive unless a company or school covers you. One commenter says they stopped registering three years ago because the companies there weren't hiring entry-level anyway. And the original poster was only planning to attend virtually, and is still gutted.

That's not one bad year. That's a market shift:

  1. Companies freeze entry-level hiring.
  2. Students see fewer employers and skip registering.
  3. Fewer attendees, weaker ROI, sponsors pull out.
  4. Revenue falls below operating costs. Event canceled.

When a community event is mostly a recruiting fair, it rises and falls with the hiring market. A community that exists for its own sake, for learning, mentoring and belonging, keeps going when the booths go dark.

What GHC promised is still worth building

In June, AnitaB.org published a first-timer's guide to GHC 26. Read it now and it lands differently. Its pitch wasn't really the expo hall. It was the feeling of walking into a room full of women who get it. Hearing a speaker name the thing you've felt for years. Leaving with confidence, momentum, and proof that you belong. Realizing you are not navigating this industry alone.

Every word of that is true. And none of it requires a convention center in Anaheim.

AnitaB.org said it best in the cancellation notice itself: GHC has always been about "more than a place or a moment on the calendar." I agree. So let's prove it.

It's worth remembering where GHC came from. Anita Borg and Telle Whitney started it in 1994 in Washington, D.C., with about 500 women in the room, and Borg had already started Systers, an email list for women in computing, back in 1987. As recently as 2002, GHC drew just 630 people. That's grassroots. That's a community before it was a brand. The belonging GHC promised was always built by people, not by sponsorship tiers, and people can build it again: in chapters, in meetups, on Discord, in free online conferences.

Community should be a distributed system

Here's what a resilient version looks like, and it already exists.

When I started PyLadies Chicago, there was no keynote stage and no expo hall. There was a room, some pizza, and people who wanted to write Python together. PyLadies grew the same way everywhere: chapter by chapter, city by city, organizer by organizer. No single chapter is load-bearing. If one goes quiet, the network routes around it.

That's the architecture worth investing in: many small nodes, low cost to join, and leaders who grow out of the community instead of being flown in for it.

Margaret Hamilton kept the mission flying

Just two weeks before GHC went dark, we lost Margaret Hamilton. She died September 30 at 90. At MIT's Instrumentation Lab she led the onboard flight software for the crewed Apollo missions, and she started calling the work "software engineering" so it would be taken as seriously as any other engineering discipline. She was also the first woman programmer on the Apollo project.

During Apollo 11's descent, the guidance computer threw 1202 alarms. It was overloaded. Hamilton's priority-driven software did exactly what it was built to do: it shed the nonessential background work, kept the critical tasks running, and Houston gave the go to land.

That's adapting under pressure, and it's the whole argument of this post. When conditions change mid-mission, you don't abort. You reprioritize. You protect what matters most and keep flying. For women in tech right now, what matters most isn't the expo hall. It's the learning, the mentoring and the belonging, and we can keep those running even when one big room goes dark.

Her daughter Lauren has said Hamilton raised her believing there were no gender barriers to what she could do. That's the inheritance. Let's keep it running.

One room to try next: PyLadiesCon, December 5–7

If GHC was on your calendar, here's one place to start.

PyLadiesCon 2026 is the fourth global PyLadies conference, and it is:

  • Free. Not "early-bird discounted." Free.
  • Online. No flight, no hotel, no visa. The organizers chose this on purpose to lower barriers for people everywhere.
  • Multilingual and multi-timezone. Sessions in English, Español, Português, Deutsch, 日本語 and 中文.
  • Hands-on. Tutorials and workshops where you build something, sprints with actual maintainers (first-time contributors welcome), open spaces, panels on Python and careers, and networking.
  • Open to everyone. No local chapter? Don't know Python yet? Come anyway.

It's run by volunteers I'd trust with anything: Georgi Ker, Mariatta, Vicky Twomey-Lee, Cristián Maureira-Fredes, Maria José Molina, Abigail Dogbe, Naa Ashiorkor Nortey and many more.

And to be clear: PyLadiesCon is one example, not the answer. Calling any single conference the gathering for women in tech overstates it, and the industry is already moving past that framing. The rooms already exist:

  • SWE's WE26: Boston, November 5–7, with 15,000+ attendees expected.
  • WiCyS: 2,000+ in person and 1,026 virtual registrants this March, plus 865 scholarships awarded.
  • The Tapia Celebration: CMD-IT/ACM's conference for diversity in computing, held in Atlanta this September.
  • Women in Data Science (WiDS): born at Stanford, now in an estimated 150+ locations worldwide, with WiDS Munich coming up December 11.
  • RLadies+: 200+ chapters in 60+ countries and over 100,000 members.
  • Lesbians Who Tech & Allies: its 14th annual LWTSUMMIT lands in New York June 7–9, 2027, with hands-on AI workshops built for every role (not just engineers), a free virtual pass, and scholarships for people between jobs.

None of them has to carry everyone. That's the point.

Reinvest, don't retreat

The GHC budget didn't evaporate. It's sitting in someone's spreadsheet right now. Here's where it can go:

If you are… Do this
A student or early-career dev who lost GHC Register for PyLadiesCon, find your local PyLadies chapter, and submit to a regional PyCon. Smaller rooms, better conversations.
A company with an unspent GHC line item Sponsor PyLadiesCon (as of this writing, the sponsor wall is still empty), fund local chapters, and send your recruiters to community events year-round, not once a year.
A senior engineer or manager Volunteer: subtitles, moderation, sprint mentoring. Or simply sponsor one person's first talk.
Anyone Donate. Small, recurring, distributed. Exactly the resilience we're talking about.
Looking for more rooms The community's own picks: WiCyS for security, the SWE conference and your local SWE chapter, and field-specific conferences (PyCon, NeurIPS) where hiring is more targeted.

IDIC, not a booth

Vulcan philosophy has a phrase for this: Infinite Diversity in Infinite Combinations. It was never meant to be one big annual gathering. It's a way of operating, every day, in every combination of people who show up.

Grace Hopper famously said it's easier to ask forgiveness than to get permission. So let's not wait for permission, or for the next big room to be rebuilt. The infrastructure is already here, and PyLadiesCon is less than two months out.

Your move, starting today

Pick one. Do it before Friday.

  1. Register for PyLadiesCon. Free, December 5–7, from wherever you are.
  2. Forward this to whoever owns your company's GHC budget. That money is looking for a home right now. Point it at PyLadiesCon sponsorship, a local chapter, or scholarships for the next room.
  3. Raise your hand to volunteer. Subtitles, moderation, sprint mentoring. An hour of yours could be someone's first open source pull request.
  4. Find or start a local chapter. Every new node makes the network stronger.
  5. Message one person who was headed to Anaheim. Tell them there's still a room for them.

The reality is real: one of our biggest rooms just went dark, and the numbers in AI are stark. But I've watched this community build something out of one room and a few pizzas more than once. We know how to do this. Let's go do it.

See you December 5–7.

Until next time: live long, Python & prosper. 🖖
